An abdominal film shows radiopaque tablets. Glucose is 140 mg/dL. The serum iron level is markedly elevated. Activated charcoal is ordered as the sole antidote.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Observation at home
N-acetylcysteine
More iron to bind the deferoxamine
Deferoxamine for systemic iron toxicity
Activated charcoal as the sole antidote
correctAnswer: Deferoxamine for systemic iron toxicity
explanation: Vomiting, shock, radiopaque tablets, and a high iron level are systemic iron poisoning, treated with deferoxamine. Charcoal binds iron poorly and is not the antidote. N-acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen. More iron increases toxicity. A lethargic, hypotensive toddler cannot go home.

scenario: A 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes had a seizure at home from glucose 28 mg/dL. His parents did not have glucagon and called an ambulance. He is now 110 mg/dL after dextrose and is awake. A1c is 7.2%. He reports two similar episodes this semester.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Tighten the target
Tell the family glucagon is unnecessary if they have juice
Add a sulfonylurea
Prescribe glucagon, teach the family, and look for why insulin is overshooting
Stop basal insulin
correctAnswer: Prescribe glucagon, teach the family, and look for why insulin is overshooting
explanation: Severe hypoglycemia needs glucagon available and a regimen review. Juice does not treat a seizure. A sulfonylurea, a tighter target, and stopping basal insulin are wrong.

scenario: A 60-year-old man is five days after a bowel resection. Temperature is 38.3°C. The incision is spreading red and tender with a small amount of pus. He is hemodynamically stable and the abdomen is soft. He reports the redness grew overnight.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Topical ointment only
Incentive spirometry only
Immediate reoperation for a leak without examining the wound
Open and drain the wound and give appropriate antibiotics
Discharge with no antibiotics
correctAnswer: Open and drain the wound and give appropriate antibiotics
explanation: Spreading erythema and pus on day 5 are a wound infection to open. Spirometry, assuming a leak without looking, ointment, and discharge miss the collection.

scenario: A 78-year-old woman with heart failure becomes short of breath after the second unit of red cells. Oxygen saturation falls to 88%. Blood pressure is 170/95 mm Hg. She has new rales and no fever, rigors, or back pain. The unit is still running.
question: Which first plan is most appropriate?
options: Stop the transfusion and give a diuretic and oxygen
Continue the unit slowly
More blood because saturation is low
Epinephrine for anaphylaxis
Heparin for pulmonary embolism without stopping the blood
correctAnswer: Stop the transfusion and give a diuretic and oxygen
explanation: Hypertension, rales, and hypoxia during transfusion without fever are circulatory overload. Stop the blood and diurese. Continuing, epinephrine, more blood, and heparin miss transfusion-associated circulatory overload.

scenario: A 23-year-old man on treatment for latent tuberculosis has a seizure after taking a bottle of isoniazid. The seizure continues after a benzodiazepine. Glucose is 100 mg/dL. He is acidotic and lethargic between convulsions. Blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg.
question: Which antidote plan is most appropriate?
options: More isoniazid
Intravenous pyridoxine, and repeat the benzodiazepine as needed
Naloxone as the isoniazid antidote
Phenytoin as the only drug
Pyridoxine withheld because a benzodiazepine was already given
correctAnswer: Intravenous pyridoxine, and repeat the benzodiazepine as needed
explanation: Isoniazid consumes pyridoxine and causes seizures that respond poorly until pyridoxine is replaced. A benzodiazepine is an adjunct, not a reason to skip the antidote. Phenytoin alone does not replete the cofactor. More isoniazid worsens the seizures. Naloxone reverses opioids, not isoniazid.

scenario: A 66-year-old man received alteplase an hour ago. Blood pressure is now 198/110 mm Hg. The neurologic examination is unchanged. A plan says not to treat pressure after the bolus because the drug is already in.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Lower systolic pressure to 100 mm Hg
Leave 198/110 untreated
Give a second dose of alteplase
Start heparin
Lower and keep blood pressure below 180/105 mm Hg for the next day
correctAnswer: Lower and keep blood pressure below 180/105 mm Hg for the next day
explanation: After alteplase, blood pressure is kept below 180/105. Leaving it, crashing it to 100, heparin, and a second lytic dose are wrong.

scenario: A 48-year-old woman has taken methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis for a year. She feels well. No blood count or liver test has been done in ten months. The refill is due. She reports no mouth sores.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Double the dose without labs
Add leflunomide the same day with no labs
Stop methotrexate forever because a year has passed
Check a blood count and liver tests before refilling, and continue folic acid
Refill with no labs because she feels well
correctAnswer: Check a blood count and liver tests before refilling, and continue folic acid
explanation: Methotrexate needs periodic blood counts and liver tests even when she feels well. A year is not a reason to stop a working drug, and doubling or adding leflunomide without labs is unsafe.

scenario: A 45-year-old man is pulled from a house fire. He is hypotensive at 80/40 mm Hg, comatose, and the lactate is 16 mmol/L. Soot is in the mouth. Oxygen saturation is low and he is being ventilated. A plan waits for a cyanide level before any antidote and gives methylene blue.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Methylene blue as the cyanide antidote
A beta blocker for the hypotension
Hydroxocobalamin now, with continued oxygen
Wait for a confirmatory cyanide level
Naloxone alone
correctAnswer: Hydroxocobalamin now, with continued oxygen
explanation: Coma, shock, and a very high lactate after smoke inhalation are treated as cyanide poisoning. Hydroxocobalamin is given immediately, with oxygen. A send-out level must not delay the antidote. Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, not cyanide. Naloxone does not reverse cyanide. A beta blocker worsens shock.

scenario: A 30-year-old woman has fever, flank pain, and vomiting that has settled. She can drink. Blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows white cells. She is not pregnant. Nitrofurantoin is prescribed because it is her usual cystitis drug.
question: Which antibiotic plan is most appropriate?
options: Nitrofurantoin for three days
Intravenous antibiotics for five days solely because the word pyelonephritis was used
No antibiotic until culture day three
A single dose of fosfomycin
Use an oral agent that reaches kidney tissue, not nitrofurantoin
correctAnswer: Use an oral agent that reaches kidney tissue, not nitrofurantoin
explanation: Nitrofurantoin and single-dose fosfomycin do not treat pyelonephritis. A stable patient can take an appropriate oral antibiotic. Waiting three days is unsafe, and admission is not mandatory when she can drink and is stable.
